Recommendation System 6 - Vector Similarity Search Using ScaNN
In this post, we’ll explore how to perform fast vector similarity searches using ScaNN. The BruteForce method used in implementing the Retrieval Model computed the dot product with all movie embedding vectors and retrieved the Top K items with the highest dot product values. This approach can lead to severe performance degradation when the total number of items exceeds hundreds of millions. TFRS provides the ScaNN package, which can be used alongside it to achieve fast and accurate results.
ANN
Unlike BruteForce, ScaNN uses various optimization techniques and doesn’t compare against all embedding vectors. As a result, the similar vectors found by ScaNN are approximations rather than exact values. This type of vector similarity search is called ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor).
There are various methods to evaluate similarity between vectors, such as Euclidean distance or cosine similarity. The ANN method that finds results with the highest dot product values, commonly used in recommendation systems, is called MIPS (Maximum Inner Product Search). MIPS employs two main optimization techniques: reducing computation and quantization.
Reducing Computation
To enable fast search, the amount of computation must be reduced. This involves using tree-based search algorithms or hashing algorithms to exclude distant vectors and compute distances only between nearby vectors.
Quantization
Quantization here refers to a compression technique that reduces the number of possible values used to represent data, thereby shrinking the memory footprint of vectors. When data is compressed, not only does the memory usage for hundreds of millions of vectors decrease, but the memory bandwidth to the CPU is also reduced, maximizing the CPU’s computational power.
ScaNN
ScaNN is a state-of-the-art open-source vector similarity search library announced by Google Research in 2020, offering faster and more effective performance. Looking at the performance comparison graphs from the blog and benchmarking the ANN performances in , you can clearly see its superiority.
ScaNN uses the optimization techniques described above. It quickly finds similar vectors using Asymmetric Hashing and compresses data more accurately and efficiently through a method called Anisotropic Vector Quantization.

Diving Deeper into ScaNN
ScaNN’s Search Process
First, let’s look at the search process. When given a query vector to search, ScaNN finds similar vectors in the following 3 steps:
1.
Partitioning: ScaNN pre-partitions the entire dataset (grouping similar values together) and identifies partitions similar to the query vector to pass to the next step.
2.
Scoring: It measures distances between the data within the partitions and computes the scores. At this point, it uses Asymmetric Hashing (AH) to calculate values that are fast and nearly identical to the actual distances (near-perfect).
3.
Rescoring: Based on the distances of the vectors filtered through steps 1 and 2, it selects the Top K values. Then, it measures the exact distances again and sorts them.
Tuning ScaNN
We’ll explore how to adjust the constructor arguments of the ScaNN class to increase speed at the cost of accuracy or vice versa.
Among these, let’s examine the parameters for performance tuning.
•
query_model: A model that converts inputs into embedding vectors.
•
name: Layer name.
•
k: Specifies the default number of similar vectors to retrieve.
•
num_leaves: Specifies the number of partitions to divide into.
•
num_leaves_to_search: Specifies how many partitions from the partitioning step to pass to the scoring step.
•
dimensions_per_block (default 2): Data compression ratio; higher values increase compression but reduce accuracy.
•
num_reordering_candidates: In the rescoring step, after selecting Top K, it re-measures exact distances and re-sorts. This parameter specifies the number to filter during rescoring. Larger values yield more accurate results but slower speed. If not specified, rescoring is skipped. This value must always be larger than k, the number of recommendations.
•
parallelize_batch_searches: Processes queries in parallel.
For example, if num_leaves is 100 and num_leaves_to_search is 10, it divides the whole into 100 partitions and only searches 10 of them, so only the top 10% that seem promising are searched. If num_leaves is 1000 and num_leaves_to_search is 100, it similarly searches only 10%, but with greater accuracy.
Rules of Thumb
There are quite a few tuning parameters, but the ScaNN GitHub recommends the following approaches:
1.
For datasets with 20,000 or fewer items, use Brute-Force. → Using ScaNN would actually be less efficient.
2.
For datasets with 100,000 or fewer items, use AH Scoring and Rescoring without partitioning → Partitioning isn’t necessary.
3.
For 100,000+ items, use partitioning along with AH Scoring and Rescoring.
4.
When using AH-Tree, set dimensions_per_block to 2.
5.
When using partitioning, num_leaves should roughly be the square root of the data size.
Applying the Recommendations
Let’s apply the recommendations. Since TFRS’s ScaNN layer always uses AH Scoring, we can fix dimensions_per_block at 2, set num_leaves to the square root of the data size (or use BruteForce if too small), and then adjust num_leaves_to_search and num_reordering_candidates based on performance and accuracy to find the right trade-off.
We’ll use recall as the metric for comparing performance. It treats the BruteForce Top 100 results as the true labels and measures how well they match the ScaNN Top 100. Let’s test by varying the parameters.
An interesting point is that increasing certain parameter values doesn’t always lead to performance improvements or declines. Combinations of various parameters can also yield better recall with less time.
In this post, we explored how to perform faster Retrieval in TFRS models using ScaNN. In the next post, we’ll improve the Retrieval Model and Ranking Model implemented in the previous article.
